body:
While I agree with the criticism of "secure coding" classes more being "ethical hacking" exercises in general, I don't think it's fair to so categorically state "This does not help developers." - in many organizations the lack of security awareness is one of the main issues and such a course may still be of value to developers. 

I suggest to change the sentence to "This may not necessarily help developers to write more secure code." to make it more nuanced.

comments.body:
(Disclosure: As part of my job, I run secure coding classes.)

I would agree that a blanket negative statement is unfair - I have personally seen positive impact from these classes, including students discovering and fixing vulnerabilities during the class. Awareness of attacks and how they work can be very useful - I've found that most developers want to build secure software, but often don't know what they are doing wrong. Providing an opportunity to learn about common issues and how they are exploited can have a positive impact.

Obviously, it depends on the environment, the developers, the teachers, and if the students are actually trying to learn - or if they are just going through training to check a box.

title: For Secure Development Training - "This does not help developers." is a bit harsh
